thread:
Cheng: quick heads-up — ran a long nsys capture to troubleshoot a KV-cache regression and noticed kernel timestamp drift across GPUs. nvprof timelines looked stable, but nsys shows the same kernel (matmul_kernel) jumping ~15-25ms forward intermittently. attaching logs soon.
Ben: hmm, do you have the exact nsys CLI you used? sampling vs full-trace matters a lot for timeline alignment.
Cheng: posted the command I used:
```bash
nsys profile \
  --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt \
  --output=run_kv_warmup_2026-03-15 \
  --force-overwrite \
  --duration=120 \
  --sample=periodic --sample-interval=100us \
  --capture-range=process:my_server:100-110000 \
  ./bin/kv_infer --model v3 --seq 2048 --batch 8
```
Cheng: notes: collect range brackets around the steady-state window, included osrt for thread switching markers, nvtx for our inject markers. the drift appears after the warmup bracket ends.
Alicia: can you paste the kernel timeline snippet? curious whether it's a CUDA context switch or host-side scheduling lag — osrt markers help. also which driver/runtime version?
Cheng: timeline excerpt (simplified):
```
GPU0: matmul_kernel 0-12ms | other_k 12-18ms | matmul_kernel 18-33ms | matmul_kernel 58-73ms
GPU1: matmul_kernel 0-13ms | matmul_kernel 18-33ms | other_k 33-45ms | matmul_kernel 48-63ms
```
Cheng: you can see the same kernel on GPU0 moves from 33ms to 58ms region later in the run. not just shifted sample points — whole groupings re-align.
Kai: looks like a sampling aliasing issue with the interval. try disabling periodic sampling so nsys records full ranges for CUDA kernels: `--sample=none` (if you can afford larger traces) and increase --duration to capture the full steady-state (e.g., 300s) but with capture-range to limit file size.
Ben: another angle: nvtx bracket boundaries — if the warmup bracket isn't caught precisely, the kv-cache warmup eviction might cause a pause and downstream kernel batching to shift. did you enable our KV warmup marker around the prefix? (`nvtxRangePush("kv:prefix")`)
Cheng: yes we push NVTX around warmup and around batch flush. nvtx markers align with the shift in the trace. suspect: host thread preemption + CPU-side batching heuristic kicking in when a GC-like housekeeping starts.
Alicia: try adding `--trace=nvtx,osrt` only (drop cuda trace flags) for a smaller, quicker run to validate host-side timing first. also reproduce with `nvcuda` debug env vars off/on. driver version: 535.86.10 here.
Cheng: good call — I'll run two quick captures: (1) nvtx+osrt, sample=none, 60s steady-state bracket; (2) cuda+nvtx+osrt with sample=none but shorter duration to inspect kernel alignment. will upload links.
deploy-bot: upload complete: s3://redwood-perf/4129876543/nvtx_osrt_60s.qdrep
Ben: after you have the full qdrep we can run the timeline aggregation script (tools/trace/align_kernels.py) to compute per-kernel median start variance across GPUs. that will tell us if it's systematic skew or outliers.
Kai: also worth trying `nsys profile --profile-child-processes true` in case helper processes spawn and steal CPU time for batching decisions.
Cheng: thanks — kicking off runs now. will report back with qdrep and the align_kernels output. short-term mitigation: pin batch scheduler thread to isolated CPUs to see if that eliminates the timestamp jumps.
Ben: perfect. if pinning helps, we should add an autoset flag in dedicated runtime config to pin sensitivity-critical threads for production pools.
Cheng: agreed. logging next steps here so we don't lose context. thanks all. :thumbsup:
